translation_updates.summary: Conservation of mass is the principle that the total mass of a closed system remains unchanged over time, whatever internal processes act on it. Early experimental support is attributed to Jean Rey in the seventeenth century, and Mikhail Lomonosov articulated the law in 1756, but the more influential and widely credited demonstrations came from Antoine Lavoisier's later eighteenth-century experiments, which helped displace phlogiston theory and establish quantitative chemistry. The law holds only in the classical, non-relativistic regime; at very high energies or in systems with strong gravitational fields, mass and energy conservation must be treated jointly rather than separately.

Cell theory holds that all living organisms are composed of cells, that the cell is the basic unit of structure and function in life, and that new cells arise only from pre-existing ones. The first two tenets are usually credited to Theodor Schwann and Matthias Jakob Schleiden in 1839, building on earlier microscopic observations by Robert Hooke and Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, though Schleiden's own account of new cells forming by crystallization was later abandoned. Rudolf Virchow added the third tenet in 1855, though the underlying idea had already been proposed by Robert Remak. Some modern biologists continue to debate whether non-cellular entities such as viruses should count as living, since they are an exception to the theory's central claim.

Germ theory holds that microorganisms, or pathogens, cause infectious disease, and it displaced the earlier miasma theory that attributed illness to foul air. Basic versions of the idea were proposed by Girolamo Fracastoro in 1546 and elaborated by Marcus von Plenciz in 1762, well before either found scientific acceptance. A transitional period toward acceptance began in the late 1850s with Louis Pasteur's work on fermentation and spontaneous generation, and Robert Koch extended this work in the 1880s, including formulating criteria for linking specific microorganisms to specific diseases. By the end of the 1880s miasma theory was losing ground to germ theory among scientists, and a period of rapid bacteriological discovery followed.

Uniformitarianism is the assumption that the natural laws and processes observed in the present have operated in the same way throughout the past and apply everywhere, underlying the geological maxim that the present is the key to the past. The idea originated with the geologist James Hutton in the late eighteenth century, was subsequently refined by John Playfair, and was popularized by Charles Lyell starting with his Principles of Geology in 1830; the term itself was coined by William Whewell in a review of Lyell's book. It was developed in opposition to catastrophism, which held that Earth's history was shaped mainly by sudden, large-scale upheavals. Many modern geologists no longer hold to a strict gradualist version of the idea, instead viewing Earth's history as a slow process punctuated by occasional catastrophic events.

Entropy is a thermodynamic state variable that quantifies the number of microscopic configurations, or microstates, consistent with a system's macroscopic condition. It is central to the second law of thermodynamics, which holds that the entropy of an isolated system left to evolve spontaneously cannot decrease over time, so such systems tend toward the state of highest entropy, or thermodynamic equilibrium. The concept originated in classical thermodynamics, where Rudolf Clausius defined it in 1865 as the ratio of an infinitesimal quantity of heat to temperature, and it was later given a statistical, microscopic foundation by Ludwig Boltzmann in terms of the possible arrangements of a system's atoms and molecules. Entropy is accordingly approached in two complementary ways: macroscopically, through classical thermodynamics, and microscopically, through statistical mechanics.

Bounded rationality is the idea that human decision-making is constrained by the difficulty of the problem, the cognitive capacity of the mind, and the time available, so that people typically settle for a satisfactory option rather than an optimal one. The term was coined by Herbert Simon as an alternative to the idealized rational-agent models built into expected-utility theory, and it has been used as a modeling basis across economics, political science, and related disciplines, not only within behavioral economics narrowly. Simon contrasted this satisficing approach with the classical assumption of unlimited computational and informational resources, and later researchers, including Gerd Gigerenzer, extended the concept by arguing that simple heuristics can outperform theoretically optimal procedures under real-world constraints. The concept remains actively used and debated across political science, economics, psychology, law, philosophy, and cognitive science.

The ideal type is a methodological construct developed by the sociologist Max Weber for use in comparative and interpretive social science. It is formed by selectively emphasizing certain features of a phenomenon and combining them into a unified analytical construct that does not correspond exactly to any single concrete case; Weber used the German word 'ideal' to mean the world of ideas rather than perfection or a statistical average. Because an ideal type is an admittedly artificial, one-sided construction, Weber held that its worth cannot be judged by how closely it corresponds to reality, only by its usefulness as an interpretive tool. Weber applied the method to build typologies, including four types of social action (zweckrational, wertrational, affektual, and traditional) and three ideal types of legitimate domination, using it to analyze both general phenomena, such as capitalism, and historically specific cases, such as the Protestant ethic.

verdicts.notes: generator self-flags: Deliberately avoided saying Lavoisier 'discovered' or 'founded' the law — article credits Rey with the earliest demonstration and records Lomonosov's independent 1756 priority claim, so I used 'more influential and widely credited' rather than 'first'. | The relativistic caveat (last sentence) synthesizes two separate lead paragraphs (classical-limit scope, general-relativity complication) rather than quoting either verbatim — worth a second look to confirm I didn't overstate the mc^2 / general-relativity material, which is dense. | Not fully sure the summary's framing of Lomonosov as secondary to Lavoisier matches the source's own balance — the article gives Lomonosov his own subsection and a Dorfman quote; QC may want more weight on him.

sources.quote: Credit for developing cell theory is usually given to two scientists: Theodor Schwann and Matthias Jakob Schleiden.
In 1839, Schleiden suggested that every structural part of a plant was made up of cells or the result of cells.
In 1855, Rudolf Virchow added the third tenet to cell theory.
All cells arise only from pre-existing cells
some biologists consider non-cellular entities such as viruses living organisms and thus disagree with the universal application of cell theory to all forms of life.

verdicts.notes: generator self-flags: Kept the source's 'usually given' hedge on Schwann/Schleiden credit rather than stating it flatly, per the QC ruling. | Summary omits the article's claim that Virchow may have plagiarized Remak on the third tenet ('it has been suggested that Virchow plagiarized Remak') — I judged that too uncertain/contentious for a 2-5 sentence encyclopedic summary, but flagging in case QC wants it included as a hedge rather than dropped. | The Virchow citation quote ('In 1855, Rudolf Virchow added the third tenet to cell theory.') is a plain factual sentence with no hedge of its own — the hedge about credit lives in the Remak sentence just before it, which I did not quote directly.

sources.quote: the entropy of an isolated system left to spontaneous evolution cannot decrease with time
The concept of entropy is described by two principal approaches, the macroscopic perspective of classical thermodynamics, and the microscopic description central to statistical mechanics.
In 1865, German physicist Rudolf Clausius, one of the leading founders of the field of thermodynamics, defined it as the quotient of an infinitesimal amount of heat to the instantaneous temperature.

Austrian physicist Ludwig Boltzmann explained entropy as the measure of the number of possible microscopic arrangements or states of individual atoms and molecules of a system that comply with the macroscopic condition of the system.

verdicts.notes: generator self-flags: Scoped this deliberately to thermodynamic/statistical-mechanics entropy per the ruling — the source article also covers entropy's use in information theory, economics, and cosmology, which I left out entirely; flagging in case QC wants at least a passing acknowledgment that the term is used more broadly. | The article credits William Rankine (1850) with an earlier, differently-named version of the concept before Clausius's 1865 naming — I did not mention Rankine, which slightly simplifies the history; low confidence this omission matters but noting it.

notes: Editorial batch 8 — the public-surface half of session #60 Track D. Earns the en summary + indexable flip for the seven concepts concept-wave3-v1 added, keeping the editorial gap at 0.

Regime: separated-context generation (ordered as Opus per decisions (26)/(76) — see the provenance correction below; it actually ran on claude-sonnet-5) grounded in the same fetch-corpus captures Track D QC used, then orchestrator machine QC + close-read. Machine: fetch-verify 31/31 PASS against the live pages, then re-verified against the recorded §8 anchors. Close-read: 7/7 = 100%.

★ Zero patches. Close-read found no factual error and no wording drift worth correcting — the first batch this session to need none. Both self-flagged uncertainties were checked and resolved in the generator-s favour: the Virchow/Remak point ("the idea that all cells come from pre-existing cells had already been proposed by Robert Remak") is in the source, and the summary-s decision to omit the plagiarism allegation is the conservative reading; and the Gigerenzer characterisation ("Gigerenzer proposes and shows that simple heuristics often lead to better decisions than theoretically optimal procedures") is stated almost verbatim in the article, though it took a second, deeper scan to find — the orchestrator-s first pass had surfaced only a different Gigerenzer sentence and provisionally suspected an over-attribution.

The contrast with editorial batch 7 (four patches, same session, same model, same regime) is the datum worth keeping: batch 8-s order carried seven explicit attribution rulings produced by the immediately preceding QC — who founded what, who merely popularised or extended it, which sense of a homonymous term is meant. Batch 7-s order carried two. Grounding the editorial order in the QC that just ran on the same nodes appears to be what removed the patch load; recorded as an observation from N=2, not a rule.

The one composition note the generator raised is accepted as written: the ideal-type summary-s closing sentence pairs a Wikipedia claim (four types of social action) with an SEP claim (three types of legitimate domination) that neither source states together. Both halves are individually sourced and both are consistent with concept:tripartite-classification-of-authority already in the corpus; the pairing is editorial structure, not an asserted connection.
Living-person check: no subject is a person; decision (70) does not engage.

★ PROVENANCE CORRECTION 2026-07-29 (same session, after measurement). This batch was ordered with the Agent tool parameter model:"opus" and its notes originally claimed "Opus subagent" generation per decisions (26)/(76). THAT CLAIM WAS FALSE. Measured directly at session end with two minimal probes that asked a subagent to read its own model ID from its environment: a probe requesting model:"fable" returned claude-sonnet-5, and a probe requesting model:"opus" ALSO returned claude-sonnet-5. The per-call model override was inert for this entire session — env.CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL="sonnet" in ~/.claude/settings.json is read at session start and wins over every per-call value, and removing it mid-session did not take effect. So editorial generation for this batch actually ran on claude-sonnet-5, not Opus. The orchestrator recorded the ORDER-s intent rather than the RUN-s fact, which is precisely the failure the proposal-generator contract already prevents by making the agent self-report proposed_by.model_version from its own environment. Editorial orders carried no such requirement; they now must.

★ Unintended A/B measurement, now the honest reading of this batch. Decision (26) measured editorial summaries at Opus 11/11 vs Sonnet 1/11, and decision (76) recorded editorial-on-Sonnet-5 as an explicitly UNMEASURED A/B candidate not to be adopted blindly. Because the override was inert, session #60-s four editorial batches were that A/B, run accidentally on Sonnet 5. Result as measured this session: batch 7 needed 4 patches including one factual error (Brentano-s Vienna professorship); batches 8, 9 and 10 needed zero substantive corrections, with the only batch-10 edit coming from the generator-s own flag. This is real evidence and it must not be read as an Opus result. It is also not yet a ratified routing change — decision (26)/(76) still stand until a CPO ruling, and n=4 batches from one session with a hardening order template is a weak basis on its own.
